rationale: A wins because it keeps the fragrance launch where it belongs: mostly refused until there is scent, perfumer, price, category proof, or real positioning. B's fourth angle, "Glossier adds three fragrances as it pushes into 800 more Sephora doors," is plausible but over-sold from the supplied facts; "the category Glossier is using to fill those shelves" turns three unnamed products into a strategy claim the update does not prove. A is not perfect, but "Sephora is betting more shelf on a brand whose numbers nobody outside can see" is a sharper retailer-protagonist line than B's safer shop-in-shop framing.
gaps_in_A: "Glossier is one of the few brands with a clean twelve-year arc" relies on outside context and a judgment not supplied in the update; the 2014 origin is given, but "one of the few" is not.
"suburban strip-mall retail" is an inference from Sephora at Kohl's, not a supplied fact; useful color, but it needs caution or proof.

The trend angle says the protagonist is "the cohort," then admits it needs "one other DTC-native brand's comparable move"; without that, it is a thesis waiting for reporting, not yet a pitchable angle.
gaps_in_B: "the category Glossier is using to fill those shelves" overreaches; the facts say three fragrance products launch alongside the expansion, not that fragrance is the shelf strategy.
"across two countries and two store formats, in one step" may imply simultaneity; the update does not say whether rollout is live now or phased, and B later admits it needs the timeline.
The refused line "From beauty blog to 1,400 Sephora doors..." treats the blog-to-wholesale arc as duplicate, but B throws away a legitimate feature lens that A preserves with the right proof burden.
"customer-story" is the wrong label for the Sephora at Kohl's angle; it is retailer strategy or channel format, not a customer story in any meaningful PR sense.
